name: Nicholas of Myra

seo.title: St Nicholas of Myra: the bishop, the legends and Santa Claus
seo.description: Nicholas of Myra in plain words: what is known, what was told later, the slap at Nicaea, his bones in Bari, his feast days, and how he became Santa Claus.

band.lede: A bishop of the 300s who left almost no record, and a thousand years of stories.

Small figures of Christ and the Mother of God stand by his shoulders, and rows of small saints fill the border.

who: Nicholas was bishop of Myra, a port on the south coast of today's Turkey, in the 300s. He wrote nothing, and no one who knew him wrote about him. Stories of his secret gifts and rescues spread from his tomb across East and West. His Dutch name, Sinterklaas, gave America the name Santa Claus.

tidbits.text: The poem of 1823 ends with St Nicholas “laying his finger aside of his nose” before he rises up the chimney. Moore took the gesture from Washington Irving's *History of New York*, where the saint lays “his finger beside his nose”.

cite.text: Troy Sentinel, 23 December 1823; Irving, A History of New York; Tom A. Jerman, History News Network

tidbits.text: The Coptic book of saints, read on his day, adds a footnote. He is “the true personality behind the story of St. Claus or Baba Noel”, as Arabic speakers call Father Christmas.

cite.text: Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk

tidbits.text: On his day, in much of medieval Europe, a boy was chosen bishop. He reigned until Holy Innocents' Day, 28 December.

cite.text: Britannica, “St. Nicholas”

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Patara**, a port of Lycia, say the *Lives*. The Coptic book of saints makes him a man of Myra itself. No record from his own time survives.

facts.label: Bishop of
facts.text: **Myra**, in Lycia, today **Demre in Turkey**, some time in the 300s.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: At Myra, on **6 December**. The year is unknown. The *Golden Legend* says 343, the *Catholic Encyclopedia* 345 or 352. Church calendars today say about 326 or about 342.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In a church outside Myra's walls. Most of his bones have been in **Bari**, Italy, since 1087. Venice keeps fragments.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Nicholas the Wonderworker** in the East, **Nicholas of Bari** in the West, and **Sinterklaas** in the Netherlands.

facts.label: His name
facts.text: The Greek {el|Νικόλαος}, from the words for victory and people.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Sailors, merchants, bakers, travellers and children, says the 1911 *Catholic Encyclopedia*. Also of Russia and Greece.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A bishop with **three gold balls** or purses, for the three dowries. In the West, often with **three boys in a tub**. In icons, an old bishop with a high forehead and a white beard. About 1370, Petrus de Natalibus wrote that he is mostly painted without a mitre, because he lost it for striking an Arian.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

portrait.alt: A gilded Italian panel painting: Saint Nicholas, a grey-bearded bishop with a tonsured head, looks down and to the side. He wears a richly embroidered red and green cope over white, holds a crosier, and carries a closed book with three golden balls resting on it.
portrait.credit: Saint Nicholas of Bari, Carlo Crivelli, 1472 (detail). Cleveland Museum of Art. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Carlo Crivelli
portrait.caption: Carlo Crivelli painted him in 1472 with three gold balls on his book, for the three dowries. Cleveland Museum of Art. Public domain.

west.text: The coming of his relics to **Bari**, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**. In Bari it is the feast of the Translation, when the manna is drawn.
**Catholic** optional memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The coming of his relics to Bari, in the **OCA** and other churches on the new calendar that keep it.
The same feast in the **Russian Church**, on the old calendar.
The day he died, in the **OCA** and the other Orthodox churches on the new calendar.
The **Russian Church**, on the old calendar. Also the **Coptic** Church, on 10 Kiahk in its own calendar.

feasts.note: Why two feasts? 6 December is the day he died. 9 May is the day his bones reached Bari in 1087. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so they fall on 19 December and 22 May. The OCA also remembers his birth on 29 July. The Greek Church did not take up 9 May. It saw the loss of his relics “as a sad event”, says the OCA.

traits.title: generous, and secret about it
traits.text: In the oldest full *Life*, he gave his inheritance away. The best-known gift was gold thrown by night into a poor man's house. When the father caught him, Nicholas “required him not to tell nor discover this thing as long as he lived”. The OCA's life says he always tried to give in secret.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas; OCA, 6 December

traits.title: unafraid of the powerful
traits.text: In his oldest story he stopped an execution with his own hands. Then he went to the governor who had been bribed to order it. He “found the gates closed, which anon he opened by force”, and rebuked the man until he repented. Later he threatened the emperor himself, in a dream.

cite.text: Praxis de stratelatis, as the Golden Legend tells it

traits.title: a shepherd to his city
traits.text: When three of the emperor's generals were held up in his port, he invited them to dine, “for he would keep his people from the ravin that they made”. In a famine, he talked the captains of the grain ships into sharing their cargo.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

traits.title: humble
traits.text: When sailors he had saved from a storm came to thank him, “he bade them to attribute it to the mercy of God, and to their belief, and nothing to his merits”. Chosen bishop, he tried to refuse.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

traits.title: strict with himself
traits.text: As a bishop, the *Golden Legend* says: “He woke in prayer and made his body lean, he eschewed company of women, he was humble in receiving all things, profitable in speaking, joyous in admonishing, and cruel in correcting.”

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

traits.title: hard on the old gods
traits.text: In the *Golden Legend* the people of his province still kept pagan customs, and sacrificed to Diana under a sacred tree. He made them stop, and “commanded to cut off the tree”.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

said.lede: No one who knew him wrote about him. These are voices from the centuries after.

quotes.q: …the largess which Nicholas unto the maidens gave, in order to conduct their youth to honour.
quotes.who: Dante, in *Purgatory*, about 1315. On the terrace where greed is purged, a soul praises the three dowries. Longfellow's translation.

cite.text: Dante, Purgatorio, canto 20, tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867)

quotes.q: Though he is one of the most popular saints in the Greek as well as the Latin Church, there is scarcely anything historically certain about him except that he was Bishop of Myra in the fourth century.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), St Nicholas of Myra

quotes.q: The Muscovites, who received their account of him from the Greeks, seem to pay a greater veneration to his memory than to that of any other saint who lived since the times of the apostles.

cite.text: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints, 6 December (1866 edition)

quotes.q: …no saint was more universally honoured in all Christian nations than St. Nicholas.
quotes.who: Butler, summing up the account of his relics written at Bari in 1087

cite.text: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints, 6 December (1866 edition)

moments.title: A rich couple's only child
moments.text: The *Lives* place his birth at Patara, a port on the Lycian coast, to rich Christian parents. They cannot agree on their names. The *Golden Legend* has Epiphanes and Johane. The Coptic book of saints has Epiphanius and Tona, and the OCA Theophanes and Nonna. As a baby, says the *Golden Legend*, he fed “but once on the Wednesday and once on the Friday”, the Church's fast days.

cite.text: The Golden Legend; Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk; OCA, 6 December

moments.title: Gold through the window
moments.text: His parents died and left him rich. A neighbour, a nobleman fallen into poverty, could not give his three daughters dowries, and meant to sell them into prostitution. Nicholas “threw by night secretly into the house of the man a mass of gold wrapped in a cloth”. The eldest daughter married. He did it again for the second. The third time the father lay awake, heard the gold fall and ran after him. The story is first told in the *Life* by Michael the Archimandrite. Gustav Anrich dated it between 814 and 843. Gerardo Cioffari put it about 700.

cite.text: The Golden Legend; Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998), on the dates of the Lives

moments.title: First through the door
moments.text: When the bishop of Myra died, the bishops of the province met to choose another. The bishop who led the choosing heard a voice in the night. The first man to come to church at the hour of matins, named Nicholas, was to be made bishop. He watched the doors, and Nicholas came first. He did not want it: “howbeit that he refused it strongly, yet they set him in the chair”.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

moments.title: In prison for the faith
moments.text: The later *Lives* say he was jailed and tortured under Diocletian, in the last great persecution, and freed when Constantine came to power. The story first appears about 900. The Coptic book of saints says Diocletian “tortured him severely for many years”, and that he wrote to his church from prison. Alban Butler, in 1756, noted the doubt: “The silence of other authors make many justly suspect these circumstances.”

cite.text: Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998); Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk; Butler, Lives of the Saints

moments.title: At the great council?
moments.text: Was he among the bishops who condemned Arius in 325? The *Catholic Encyclopedia* doubted it: “There is reason to doubt his presence at Nicaea, since his name is not mentioned in any of the old lists of bishops that attended this council.” The first *Life* to put him there is a eulogy by Nicetas of Paphlagonia, written before 890. His name does stand in one early list, kept by Theodore the Reader early in the 500s, but only in a manuscript of the 1200s. Gustav Anrich took it for a later addition. Gerardo Cioffari holds it genuine. Of eleven medieval copies of the lists, three name him. The Orthodox and Coptic Churches count him among the fathers of the council: “he was one of the 318 fathers assembled there”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911); Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998); Jona Lendering, Early Evidence; Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk

moments.title: The temple of Artemis
moments.text: Michael's *Life* says he destroyed the temple of Artemis at Myra. That part at least has a real setting. Myra had a temple of Artemis, shown on a coin of the emperor Gordian III. The Dutch historian Jona Lendering notes that the *Life* knows the city well. It names real places, and the granaries of its famine story have been dug up at Andriake, Myra's harbour.

cite.text: Jona Lendering, Early Evidence, after Cioffari (1987) and Blom (1998)

miracles.lede: The East calls him the Wonderworker. In the thousand years after his death, at least 50 wonder stories grew up around him. None was written down in his lifetime. Here are the oldest, mostly as the *Golden Legend* told them in the 1260s, and two later legends, marked as later. Its compiler was frank about his sources:

pledge.q: And the doctors of Greece write his legend, and some others say that Methodius the patriarch wrote it in Greek, and John the deacon translated it into Latin and adjousted thereto many things.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas, tr. William Caxton (1483), ed. F. S. Ellis (1900)

items.title: The sword taken away
items.text: Constantine sent three generals to put down a revolt. Contrary winds held them in port near Myra, and Nicholas asked them to dine. Meanwhile a governor, bribed, had condemned three innocent men. Nicholas hurried to the place of execution with the generals. The men knelt, blindfolded, with the sword raised over them. Nicholas ran in between.
items.quote: took the sword out of his hand, and threw it from him, and unbound the innocents
items.witness: The three generals, who had come with him.

cite.text: Praxis de stratelatis, as the Golden Legend tells it

items.title: The generals condemned
items.text: The generals won their war without bloodshed and came home in honour. Then jealous men at court accused them of treason, and the emperor ordered them killed that same night. In prison, one of them thought of the bishop who had stopped the sword.
items.quote: then Nepotian remembered him how S. Nicholas had delivered the three innocents

cite.text: Praxis de stratelatis, as the Golden Legend tells it

items.title: A bishop in the emperor's dream
items.text: Nicholas came to Constantine in a dream. Free these men, he said, or I will pray God to send a war against you. The emperor asked who dared to enter his palace by night and speak so. He answered:
items.quote: I am Nicholas bishop of Mirea.
items.witness: Constantine, and his prefect, who had the same dream. “Each told to other their dreams”, and the generals went free.

cite.text: Praxis de stratelatis, as the Golden Legend tells it

note.text: This is the *Praxis de stratelatis*, the story of the generals. It went round on its own long before any full *Life*. Gustav Anrich dated the version we have to between 460 and 580. Gerardo Cioffari put it earlier, before about 450. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* still tells it on his day.

cite.text: Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998); Roman Martyrology (1916), 6 December

more.title: Grain that did not run short
more.text: Famine struck Myra. Ships loaded with wheat for the emperor put in at the harbour. Nicholas asked each ship for a hundred measures. The sailors were afraid: the grain had been measured, and would be counted again at Alexandria. He promised nothing would be missing, and nothing was. The story is first told in Michael's *Life*. The *Golden Legend* says of the wheat:
more.quote: it sufficed for two years, not only for to sell, but also to sow

cite.text: The Golden Legend; Michael the Archimandrite's Life, as listed by Roger Pearse after Blom

more.title: Sailors in a storm
more.text: A ship was going down. The sailors called on Nicholas, and a man who looked like him appeared on board, helped them work the ship, and the storm died away. At his church they knew him at once, though they had never seen him. He spoke to them at sea:
more.quote: Lo! see ye me not? ye called me

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

more.title: Oil from his tomb
more.text: After his burial, the *Golden Legend* says, oil flowed from his body and healed the sick. When the next bishop was driven out, it stopped. When he came back, it flowed again. In Bari the liquid is still drawn every year.
more.quote: a fountain of oil sprang out from the head unto his feet; and unto this day holy oil issueth out of his body, which is much available to the health of sicknesses of many men

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

more.title: A later legend: the three boys
more.text: The most painted of his wonders is in none of the early Greek *Lives*, and not in the *Golden Legend*. Three young clerks on their way to school are murdered at an inn, and Nicholas raises them to life. It first appears in Latin hymns of the 1000s, a Latin play from Hildesheim of about 1100, and Wace's French *Life* of about 1150. Later tellers made the killer a butcher, and hid the boys in a salting tub. Wace's version begins, in our translation:
more.quote: Three clerks were going to school

cite.text: Wace, Life of St Nicholas, about 1150; Roger Pearse, after Joel Fredell and Charles W. Jones

more.title: A later legend: the boy carried home
more.text: A rich man named his son {la|Deus dedit}, God gave, and kept the feast of St Nicholas every year. The boy was captured by raiders and made to serve their king as cupbearer. A year later, on the feast day, he sighed at the thought of home. The king mocked him. Then a great wind shook the house.
more.quote: the child was ravished with the cup, and was set tofore the gate where his father held the solemnity of S. Nicholas

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

doubt.title: Doubted, and defended
doubt.text: The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1911 was blunt: “The numerous miracles St. Nicholas is said to have wrought, both before and after his death, are outgrowths of a long tradition.” In 1913 and 1917 the German scholar Gustav Anrich argued that the real Nicholas was lost beyond recovery. Jona Lendering points out that several stories have twins in Philostratus's *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, a pagan sage's life written in the 200s. Apollonius too gives a poor man dowries for his daughters, saves a man from death, and is seen in two places at once. Others defend the oldest *Life*. Gerardo Cioffari, in 1987, and Aart Blom, in 1998, found its places real. Lendering concludes that the dowry story is simply true. It has no miracle in it, and its care for three young women fits the 300s better than the 800s.

cites.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), St Nicholas of Myra
Jona Lendering, Early Evidence, St. Nicholas Center

words.note: He wrote nothing that survives. These are the words the stories give him, in the *Golden Legend* as William Caxton put it into English in 1483, edited by F. S. Ellis in 1900.

feature.kicker: To the captains of the grain ships
feature.q: Do this that I have said to you, and I promise, in the truth of God, that it shall not be lessed or minished when ye shall come to the garners.
feature.ctx: Myra was starving. The captains feared to give away the emperor's wheat, because it would be measured again at Alexandria.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

quotes.who: To the bishop waiting at the church door, who then told him he would be bishop of Myra.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

quotes.q: Thou enemy of God, corrupter of the law, wherefore hast thou consented to so great evil and felony, how darest thou look on us?
quotes.who: To the governor who had taken a bribe to put three innocent men to death.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

quotes.q: Wherefore hast thou taken these three princes with so great wrong, and hast judged them to death without trespass?
quotes.who: To the emperor Constantine, in a dream.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

myths.claim: He punched Arius at the Council of Nicaea.
myths.truth: No early source says so. The story first appears about 1370, in a Latin book of saints by Petrus de Natalibus. There, as an old man, he strikes {la|quemdam Arrianum}, an Arian, on the jaw, and loses his mitre and pallium for it. Arius himself first takes the blow in a Greek *Life* by a monk named Damaskenos, printed in 1570. It was a slap, not a punch. The scene became part of Orthodox icons, and the OCA tells it as tradition: he “struck him upon the face”, and Christ and the Mother of God gave him back his Gospel and his bishop's stole. The historian Jona Lendering thinks a memory may lie behind it: “this anecdote is embarrassing, and this is a reason why it is unlikely to have been invented”.

cite.text: Roger Pearse (2015), after Gustav Anrich, Hagios Nikolaos (1913); OCA, 6 December; Jona Lendering, Early Evidence

myths.claim: He was abbot of Holy Sion, a monastery founded by his uncle, the bishop.
myths.truth: That belongs to another saint: Nicholas of Sion, abbot of Holy Sion near Myra and bishop of Pinara, in the 500s. His own *Life*, written about 564, speaks of the tomb of the older Nicholas. A Greek writer of the 800s or 900s wove the two lives into one, and the joined story is still told, as in the OCA's life.

cite.text: Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998); OCA, 6 December

myths.truth: No *Life* says so. In the later *Lives* he is jailed and tortured, and lives to go home. He dies in peace at Myra. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* calls him “bishop and confessor”, the old title for a saint who was not a martyr.

cite.text: Roman Martyrology (1916), 6 December; the Golden Legend; Coptic synaxarium, 10 Kiahk

circle.name: Constantine the Great
circle.text: The first Christian emperor. In the oldest story told of Nicholas, the bishop comes to him in a dream and saves three of his generals from execution.

cite.text: Praxis de stratelatis; the Golden Legend

circle.name: Nepotian, Ursyn and Apollyn
circle.text: Constantine's three generals, as the *Golden Legend* names them. They watched Nicholas stop an execution. Later, condemned themselves, they called on him.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

circle.name: Arius
circle.text: The priest of Alexandria whose teaching the Council of Nicaea condemned in 325. The story that Nicholas slapped him is first told in the 1500s.

cite.text: Roger Pearse (2015), after Gustav Anrich

circle.name: Nicholas of Sion
circle.text: Abbot of Holy Sion near Myra and bishop of Pinara, in the 500s. His *Life*, written about 564, speaks of the tomb of the older Nicholas. Later writers merged the two men into one.

cite.text: Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998)

death.big: He died at Myra on 6 December, some time in the 300s. No record from his own time gives the year.
paras: As the *Golden Legend* tells it, he prayed the Lord to send His angels, and saw them coming. He began Psalm 31, {la|In te Domine speravi}, and died saying its fifth verse. The book puts his death in 343.

He was buried in a church outside the city walls. Jona Lendering notes that Roman law still forbade burials inside a city in the early 300s. So the site of the tomb fits a cult that began soon after his death. The church over it still stands in Demre.

later.title: The first sure signs of him
later.text: Two witnesses of the 500s show that his name was already honoured. In Constantinople the emperor Justinian built “a shrine to St. Priscus and St. Nicholas, an entirely new creation of his own”, says the historian Procopius. And the *Life of Nicholas of Sion*, written about 564, speaks of the tomb of Nicholas at Myra.

cite.text: Procopius, Buildings, Book 1, chapter 6, tr. H. B. Dewing (1940); Roger Pearse, after Aart Blom (1998)

items.k: His last words, in the Golden Legend
items.q: Lord, into Thine hands I commend my spirit
items.ctx: The words of Psalm 31:5, which Jesus prayed on the cross.

cite.text: The Golden Legend, Life of St Nicholas

extras.title: His bones: from Myra to Bari
extras.lede: In 1087 sailors from Bari carried most of his bones across the sea. They are still there, and every May a little liquid is drawn from the tomb.

items.title: The raid of 1087
items.text: By then the Turks held Lycia. Merchants of Bari, sailing home from Antioch, put in near Myra in April 1087. Forty-seven armed men went up to the church, where four monks kept the tomb. They offered the monks 300 gold coins, and the monks refused. So the men bound them and broke open the tomb. The townspeople ran to the shore too late. On 9 May 1087 the relics were carried into Bari. To the men of Bari it was a rescue: they meant, says the OCA, “to save the relics of Saint Nicholas”. To the Greeks it was a loss. Alban Butler, a Catholic priest writing in 1756, said the raid “could only be justified by the laws of a just war”, together with the fear that the Turks would profane the relics.
items.quote: they opened it and found the bones swimming in the oil, and they bare them away honourably into the city of Bari

cite.text: The Golden Legend; OCA, 9 May; Butler, Lives of the Saints; Britannica

items.title: The manna
items.text: A clear liquid gathers in his tomb. The Greeks call it myron, and Bari calls it manna. Each 9 May since 1980 it has been drawn out in front of a Catholic and an Orthodox bishop: no more than about 50 ml a year. Mixed with blessed water, it is bottled for the sick. Scientists at the University of Bari found in 1925 that it is water. *Britannica* calls it most likely condensation, since the tomb lies below ground in a port city. The basilica's own study centre answers that the casket has been proven watertight. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1911 still called it oil:
items.quote: an oily substance, known as Manna di S. Nicola, which is highly valued for its medicinal powers, is said to flow from them

cite.text: St. Nicholas Center, Devotion and Use of Manna; Britannica, on the manna; Catholic Encyclopedia (1911)

items.title: Venice, and a bone in Illinois
items.text: Bari has most of his bones, but not all. The church of San Nicolò al Lido in Venice keeps as many as 500 fragments. An anatomical study found they fit with the bones in Bari, as if from one body. In 2017 Oxford scientists dated one of the smaller relics: a piece of pelvis kept at Morton Grove, Illinois, which had come from Lyon. It dates from the 300s. Bari has the upper part of the left hip bone. This piece is from the lower part. The scientists claimed no more than that:
items.quote: Science is not able to definitely prove that it is, it can only prove that it is not

cite.text: University of Oxford, press release of 5 December 2017

extras.title: How he became Santa Claus
extras.lede: Each step is in print. How the steps join is argued over. Here are the texts, and each side in its own words.

items.title: A children's saint
items.text: In the Middle Ages his feast became a schoolboys' day. Wace, in his French *Life* of about 1150, links it to the story of the three boys. After the Reformation his feast faded in Protestant lands, but not in Holland, where he stayed Sinterklaas. Wace, in George McKnight's English of 1917:
items.quote: Because he did such honor to schoolboys, they celebrate this day by reading and singing and reciting the miracles of St. Nicholas.

cite.text: Wace, Life of St Nicholas, as quoted by George H. McKnight (1917), in Roger Pearse; Britannica

items.title: Irving's New York
items.text: Washington Irving's comic *History of New York*, of 1809, made St Nicholas the patron of the old Dutch town. In later editions, from 1812, Irving gave him more to do. In the text we read today he rides over the treetops, drops presents down chimneys, and in a dream lays “his finger beside his nose”. The book says:
items.quote: for the good St. Nicholas has ever been a great giver of gifts, particularly to children

cite.text: Washington Irving, A History of New York, book 2 (later edition); Tom A. Jerman, History News Network

items.title: The poem of 1823
items.text: On 23 December 1823 the *Troy Sentinel*, a New York paper, printed an unsigned poem, “Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas”. By the mid-1800s it was known as the work of Clement Clarke Moore, a New York professor. It has a sleigh, eight reindeer and a trip down the chimney. Two of the reindeer were first called “Dunder and Blixem”. The poem itself never says Santa Claus. It says St. Nicholas and St. Nick. The editor's note above it says “Sante Claus”. Two years before, a New York booklet had shown “Santeclaus” in a sleigh pulled by a flying reindeer.
items.quote: He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laugh'd when I saw him in spite of myself

cite.text: Troy Sentinel, 23 December 1823; Tom A. Jerman, History News Network

items.title: Who made Santa?
items.text: The older answer is that Dutch settlers brought Sinterklaas to New Amsterdam. *Britannica* says so, and so does the Episcopal Church: “his name was brought to America by the Dutch colonists in New York”. In 1954 Charles W. Jones answered that there is no proof the colonists kept the custom. He gave the credit to Irving: “Without Irving there would be no Santa Claus.” In 2020 Tom A. Jerman answered Jones in turn. Irving's gift-giving lines came in 1812, he points out, and Santa grew from German winter figures by way of two New York poems. In his words, “St. Nicholas and Santa Claus were two different characters”.

cite.text: Britannica; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; Charles W. Jones (1954); Tom A. Jerman, History News Network

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: 6 December, in the Church of England

paras: His honour began at his tomb in Myra. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* notes that his name occurs in the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, the Orthodox Church's usual Sunday service. The Russian Church honours him in particular every Thursday of the year, says the OCA.

Rome's calendar of 1969 notes that the Byzantine and Coptic rites keep 6 December, the day he was laid to rest. In the West, it says, his feast spread from the 900s, most of all after his relics came to Bari in 1087. The old *Roman Martyrology* gives him this line:

quotes.q: At Myra, the metropolis of Lycia, the birthday of St. Nicholas, bishop and confessor, of whom it is related, among other miracles, that, while at a great distance from the emperor Constantine, he appeared to him in a vision and moved him to mercy so as to deter him from putting to death some persons who had implored his assistance.
quotes.who: The *Roman Martyrology*, 1916 edition, for 6 December. A saint's birthday is the day he died.

cite.text: The Roman Martyrology (1916)
